content: Conversion of a Three-Wheeler into a Low-Cost Passenger Vehicle for Indian Market
Frugal Engineering in Practice: A Case Study on the Conversion of a Three-Wheeler into a Low-Cost Passenger Vehicle for the Indian Market
Need for Affordable Travel in India
Many people in India want personal transport, but most cars are too expensive.
Three-wheeled auto-rickshaws are cheap but don't have a closed cabin, aren't very stable, and can't carry many people.
Even cheapest cars are too costly for many, creating a big "affordability gap"
How "Frugal Engineering" helps:
Clever, making smart choices, and keeping costs very low
Focus on making things work well with limited money and resources
Goal: Build a four-wheeled vehicle that's much cheaper than current cars
Our Method
We followed frugal engineering rules, focusing on keeping costs down and using materials found locally.
We converted a regular Bajaj RE Diesel three-wheeler into a four-wheeled car
Key Design Choices
Making Frame Longer (Chassis Extension):
What We Did: We attached the front half of another used Bajaj RE chassis
Used cheap, ready-made parts, which helped line up the suspension correctly without needing special tools.
Steering System:
What We Did: Used rack-and-pinion steering system.
Why It Was Smart: This gave a more car-like steering feel and used cheap, standard parts
Body Panels (Outer Shell):
What We Did: Used 1.2 mm thick Galvanized Iron (GI) sheets.
Why It Was Smart: These sheets are cheap, easy to find, and simple to work with using basic tools
Brake System:
What We Did: Installed a tandem master cylinder.
Why It Was Smart: This is needed to operate brakes on all four wheels and adds a safety feature by having a backup.
What to Do Next
Make it safe with a full safety program
Do detailed analysis to check its strength, how weight is spread, and how it would handle a crash.
Perform real crash tests to make sure the structure protects people.
Make sure it follows all rules and laws so it can be registered and driven legally
More Research Needed
Figure out the exact cost of every part (Bill of Materials).
Improve the design and materials to make it lighter and use less fuel.
Measure noise, vibration, and shakiness more accurately and do more road tests.
See if people would actually buy and use it, and if it can be made on a larger scale.
